newsitem.title: UK: IRA shoots dead two Northern Ireland policemen.
newsitem.headline: IRA shoots dead two Northern Ireland policemen.

text.p: Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas shot dead two Northern Ireland policemen in an ambush on Monday, fuelling fears the British-ruled province could face a return to widespread sectarian violence.
Britain and Ireland united in condemnation of the attack and London re-imposed a ban on contact with the IRA's Sinn Fein political arm that had been eased recently.
As Protestant leaders appealed to hardliners in their community not to retaliate, British Prime Minister Tony Blair accused republicans of sickening "cynicism and hypocrisy".
Blair, who has tried to galvanise the province's floundering peace efforts since coming to office on May 1, ruled out any fresh meeting between government officials and Sinn Fein.

"It is impossible to interpret this latest attack as anything but a signal that Sinn Fein and the IRA are not interested in peace and democracy," Blair said in a statement in Amsterdam where he was attending a European Union summit.
"There is obviously no question of a further meeting with Sinn Fein in these circumstances," declared Blair, adding that London's efforts for peace in the province would continue.

Bertie Ahern, tipped to be appointed Ireland's new Prime Minister later this month when parliament meets after recent election successes by his Fianna Fail party, also assailed the IRA over the double-murder.
He denounced it as "an evil, irresponsible and provocative action" that deliberately undermined what were hopeful efforts to restore the peace process.
"No democratic Irish government, present or future, is going to be swayed or intimidated by acts of terrorism," he declared.
Outgoing Prime Minister John Bruton also bemoaned the attack, calling it "deliberately provocative."

The officers were on routine foot patrol near the centre of the busy town of Lurgan, southwest of Belfast, when gunmen shot them at close range. A doctor ran from a nearby surgery to help but the men were already dead.
Both men were married with young children.
A caller using an IRA code word rang a Belfast radio station and said the organisation's "North Armagh Brigade" had "carried out this morning's attack".
British Northern Ireland Minister Mo Mowlam, speaking before the IRA's admission, said the killings were an outrage.
"At a time when Northern Ireland is holding its breath and hope for peace, those intent on evil have struck," Mowlam said.
"The government resolutely condemns this atrocity but we will not be intimidated into weakening our resolution to bring about a peaceful Northern Ireland in which all can share."
Since Labour won power in May 1, government officials have held two meetings with Sinn Fein to clarify conditions under which they could be admitted to the talks.

Mainstream Irish nationalist and Protestant unionist parties said that the ambush was intended to increase divisions during an annually volatile period of street parades by pro-British Protestant groups.
They appealed to Protestant "Loyalist" guerrillas, who have operated a shaky truce since October 1994, not to strike back and worsen the province's difficulties.
David Trimble, leader of the Ulster Unionists, said the murder was bound to inflame tensions and appealed for calm.
"I would ask Loyalists not to play the IRA's game. Now is the time to draw back from the brink."
